title: What We Are Building
text:
The learning and analysis tools

Learn
Learn is the main teaching section of the site.
Each lesson starts with a real question, uses a position as an example, and explains the main idea in plain language. The goal is not only to show the best move. It is to help you recognize the same idea when a different position comes up in one of your own games.


Explain
Explain lets you enter a position and see analysis from GNU and Sage.
Engines are very good at ranking moves, but their output does not always explain why one choice is better. We want to improve that by building a simple, interpretable model that connects engine results to features players can recognize, such as the race, board strength, anchors, primes, contact, and threats.
The explainer will not replace the engines. It will help turn their results into something easier to learn from.


Match Predictor
Match Predictor uses match data to explore how differences in Performance Rating, or PR, affect match results.
It is also meant to be fun. Before a big match, you can compare the players, see what the data suggests, and build some excitement around the matchup. It will never know who is going to win, because dice and match situations still matter, but it can give useful context.

title: What We Are Building
text:
Engine comparison and research

GNU vs Sage
GNU vs Sage compares two backgammon bots by having them play and then studying where their decisions differ.
The match results are interesting on their own, but the project also helps the rest of the site. Engine disagreements can become Learn lessons, detailed Research posts, or examples for improving the explainer model.
The code and data are being organized so the results can be checked and reproduced, not just posted as a scoreboard.


Research
Research is where we can go into more detail.
It will include articles and blog-like posts about what we are planning, what we are testing, what we have learned, and what still needs work. It is also where we can share extra charts, methods, and explanations that would make the main pages too crowded.
The front page should stay clear and easy to follow. Research is for readers who want to look deeper.

title: What We Are Building
text:
Open-source tools
Several open-source projects support the website.

engine-kit
engine-kit provides helper functions for working with board positions and bot services. It gives the different engines and applications a common way to describe the same position, move, cube state, and match situation.


engine-benchmark
engine-benchmark contains the code used to run and reproduce the bot-versus-bot matches. This is where the GNU vs Sage results can be generated, checked, and repeated.


The Explain app
The position explainer on the website is also open source. That means its analysis and explanation system can be inspected and improved over time.


backgammonboard
backgammonboard is an R library for drawing backgammon positions. We use it for Learn lessons, match analysis, bot comparisons, and Research posts.


backgammoncalculator
backgammoncalculator is an R library for reusable backgammon calculations. It supports lessons, match analysis, bot results, and research without requiring the same calculations to be rebuilt for every project.

title: What We Are Building
text:
How it fits together
A GNU vs Sage match may uncover an interesting position. That position may become a Research post, a new Learn lesson, or an example used to improve Explain. The same open-source tools help us draw the board, run the analysis, check the results, and publish what we learned.
That is what we are building: a place to learn the game, explore difficult positions, follow interesting experiments, and understand more of what the engines are seeing.

#2 terms




10-Percent Doubling Rule



10-Percent Doubling Rule is a race-cube shortcut: the player on roll can generally double when their adjusted count is within about 10 percent of the other player’s count. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





8-9-12 Doubling Rule



Players use 8-9-12 Doubling Rule to describe a race-cube guideline: double at about 8 percent behind, redouble at 9 percent, and take up to roughly 12 percent behind. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture







A26 terms




ABT



ABT stands for American Backgammon Tour, a series of tournament events in the United States. Players may see the abbreviation in tournament schedules, standings, and community discussion.


Category: Organizations and Community





Ace



Ace describes the number 1 on a die. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Ace-Point Game



In backgammon, Ace-Point Game refers to a late holding game in which a player keeps the other player’s one-point and waits for a bearoff shot. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Acey-Deucey



Also called: Binache, Catalin


In backgammon, Acey-Deucey refers to a family of backgammon variants, often associated with U.S. military play, in which 1-2 has special powers. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.


Category: Variants and History





Acting Captain



Acting Captain is used in a chouette. It is a temporary captain who makes the plays when the regular captain cannot act. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Action Play



Action Play is a move intended to create contact, exchanges, or tactical complications. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Checker Play and Tactics





Action Position



Players use Action Position to describe a volatile position with many immediate tactical possibilities and large equity swings. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Strategy and Position Types





Active Builder



In backgammon, Active Builder refers to a spare checker that can help make an important point on the next roll. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Checker Play and Tactics





Advanced Anchor



Players use Advanced Anchor to describe an anchor on the other player’s four-point or five-point. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Strategy and Position Types




Learn more (1)



The Main Game Plans








Advanced Level



Players use Advanced Level to describe a tournament or teaching division for strong, experienced players below the top open level. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Ahead in the Count



Ahead in the Count means having the lower pip count and therefore being ahead in the race. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Analysis and Probability





Ahead in the Race



Ahead in the Race means needing fewer total pips than the other player to bear off all checkers. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Race and Bearoff





Ammunition



Ammunition describes checkers positioned where they can attack blots or build points. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Analog Clock



Analog Clock is a mechanical chess-style clock with hands rather than a digital display. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Anchor



Also called: Holding Point


Anchor is a made point in the other player’s home board or outer board that gives safety and contact. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Strategy and Position Types





Annotated Match



Players use Annotated Match to describe a recorded match accompanied by explanations of checker plays and cube decisions. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Match and Tournament Play





Annotation



Annotation describes written or spoken analysis explaining decisions in a recorded game or match. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Anti-Joker



In backgammon, Anti-Joker refers to an exceptionally unlucky roll that sharply damages a position. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Army



Players use Army to describe a player’s full group of 15 checkers. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Around the Corner



Around the Corner means movement from the other player’s outer board into the player’s own outer board. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Match and Tournament Play





Asset



Players use Asset to describe a useful positional feature, such as an anchor, prime, strong board, or flexible builder. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Attack



The action called Attack is to hit or threaten opposing blots, generally near or inside your home board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Attack Zone



Attack Zone is the points on your side of the board from which checkers can support a blitz. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Attacking Game



Players use Attacking Game to describe a game plan based on hitting, closing points, and keeping opposing checkers on the bar. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Automatic Doubles



Also called: Automatic, Automatics


Automatic Doubles is an optional money-game rule that raises the initial cube value when both players roll the same opening number. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Cube and Scoring





Awkward Number



In backgammon, Awkward Number refers to a roll that cannot be played constructively and forces a positional concession. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture







B45 terms




Back Game



In backgammon, Back Game refers to a strategy based on holding two or more points deep in the other player’s home board and waiting for a late shot. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Strategy and Position Types




Learn more (1)



The Main Game Plans








Backgammon



Also called: Triple Game


The term Backgammon refers to the game itself, or a triple-value win when the loser has borne off nothing and still has a checker on the bar or in the winner’s home board. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture




Learn more (3)



Reading Positions and Engine Analysis


What the Cube Is Really Asking

Backgammon Board



Also called: Board


Backgammon Board describes the playing surface with 24 narrow points arranged in four quadrants and divided by the bar. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Backgammon Server



Players use Backgammon Server to describe an online service that hosts backgammon games, matches, ratings, or tournaments. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.


Category: Software and Online Play





Baffle Box



Players use Baffle Box to describe a device that randomizes dice by making them tumble through internal baffles before reaching the board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Bakelite



Players use Bakelite to describe an early hard plastic sometimes used for vintage backgammon checkers and equipment. The term is mainly historical and may not be common in modern play.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Banana Split



In backgammon, Banana Split refers to a very large split of the back checkers, typically exposing both as distant blots. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Checker Play and Tactics





Bankroll



Bankroll describes money set aside specifically for playing or wagering. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Bar



Also called: Rail, Rim, Roof


The term Bar refers to the central divider where hit checkers wait until they can re-enter. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Bar-Point



In backgammon, Bar-Point refers to a player’s seven-point, right away beside the bar. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Barabino



Barabino is a traditional Italian tables game related to backgammon. The rules or history are different from standard modern backgammon.


Category: Variants and History





Battle of Primes



In backgammon, Battle of Primes refers to a position in which both players have strong primes trapping opposing checkers. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Strategy and Position Types





Bear In



Also called: Bear On, Move In


The action called Bear In is to move all remaining checkers into your home board before bearing off. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Race and Bearoff





Bear Off



Also called: Bearoff, Go Out, Move Off, Off (the Board), Take Off, Throw Off


The action called Bear Off is to remove checkers from the board after all 15 are in your home board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Race and Bearoff





Bearoff Database



In backgammon, Bearoff Database refers to a precomputed table of exact or near-exact results for bearoff positions. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Race and Bearoff





Beaver



Also called: Beavers


Beaver is used in money play. It is an immediate redouble made by the player who accepts a double while keeping ownership of the cube. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Behind in the Race



Also called: Behind in the Count


Behind in the Race means needing more total pips than the other player to bear off all checkers. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Race and Bearoff





Bertha



Bertha is traditional slang for the roll 6-3. The term is mainly historical and may not be common in modern play.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





BIBA



BIBA stands for British Isles Backgammon Association, a tournament and membership organization. Players may see the abbreviation in connection with organized backgammon in the United Kingdom.


Category: Organizations and Community





Big Play



Big Play is an aggressive play that accepts more immediate risk for greater positional gain. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Checker Play and Tactics





Blitz



Also called: Wipeout


In backgammon, Blitz refers to an attacking plan that repeatedly hits and closes home-board points to trap opposing checkers on the bar. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Strategy and Position Types




Learn more (1)



The Main Game Plans








Block



Block means to restrict an opposing checker by occupying points in front of it. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Blockade



In backgammon, Blockade refers to a connected group of made points that obstructs opposing checkers. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Blocking Game



Also called: Blocking Backgammon


In backgammon, Blocking Game refers to a strategy focused on building points or a prime in front of opposing checkers. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Blot



Also called: Exposed Checker, Loose Checker


Players use Blot to describe a lone checker on a point, vulnerable to being hit. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Checker Play and Tactics





Blot-Hitting Contest



Players use Blot-Hitting Contest to describe a tactical sequence in which both players repeatedly hit exposed checkers. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Checker Play and Tactics





Blue game



In backgammon, Blue game refers to a collusive cheating arrangement in which players secretly cooperate against others. This term belongs in a rules, ethics, or historical explanation and should not be presented as acceptable conduct.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture


Usage note: Include only in an ethics or historical context, not as recommended conduct.





Blunder



Players use Blunder to describe a large checker-play or cube error, often defined by analysis software as losing at least 0.080 equity. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Board Setup



Also called: Board Layout, Layout


Board Setup describes the orientation of the board, points, checkers, bar, and bearoff trays for play. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Bold Play



In backgammon, Bold Play refers to an aggressive move that leaves hittable blots to pursue a stronger objective. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Checker Play and Tactics





Bot



Players use Bot to describe a computer program that plays or analyzes backgammon. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.


Category: Software and Online Play





Box



Box is used in a chouette. It is the player competing alone against the team. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Boxcars



Also called: Boxes, Boys (The Boys)


The term Boxcars refers to the roll 6-6. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Break a Point



Also called: Break


Break a Point means to move one or both checkers away from a made point so it is no longer owned. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Break a Prime



The action called Break a Prime is to open a point in a prime, allowing a trapped checker a possible escape route. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Strategy and Position Types





Break Contact



Also called: Disengage, No Contact


Break Contact means to move all checkers past the other player’s checkers so no further hits are possible. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Checker Play and Tactics





Break One's Board



The action called Break One's Board is to open one or more made points in your home board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Broken Prime



In backgammon, Broken Prime refers to a group of blocking points with at least one gap inside it. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Strategy and Position Types





Bronstein Clock



Bronstein Clock is a game clock that restores up to a fixed delay after each move, so routine move time is not charged. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Build One's Board



The action called Build One's Board is to make additional points in your home board. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Builder



Also called: Dilly Builder


Builder is a checker positioned to help make an important point on a future roll. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Checker Play and Tactics





Bury a Checker



Bury a Checker means to move a checker deep onto a low home-board point where it has little future use. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Busted Back Game



Busted Back Game is a mistimed back game whose anchors or checkers must collapse before a useful shot appears. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Strategy and Position Types





Bye



Bye refers to automatic advancement in a tournament round without playing a match. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





BYOB



BYOB stands for “bring your own board.” It is an instruction sometimes used for informal events. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture







C58 terms




Calcutta Auction



Players use Calcutta Auction to describe a tournament side auction in which participants bid for financial interests in players or teams. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





California Rule



California Rule is a local chouette convention that allows a player to decline joining a cube decision under specified conditions. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Candlesticks



Players use Candlesticks to describe an inflexible distribution with tall stacks on a few points and too few useful spare checkers. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Captain



Captain is used in a chouette. It is the team member who rolls the dice and makes the checker plays against the box. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Cash a Game



Cash a Game means offering a double that the other player should pass. The game ends with the pass, and the doubler wins the value shown on the cube before the offer.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Catchers



Catchers describes checkers placed to cover escape rolls or hit a runner trying to pass. Players may see this term in strategy discussions, match records, or analysis software.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Centered Cube



Also called: Cube in the Middle


Centered Cube is a doubling cube that still sits in the middle and belongs to neither player. Either player may offer the first double.


Category: Cube and Scoring





Championship Division



Championship Division describes the highest-skill division in a tournament, also called the open or main division. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Match and Tournament Play





Chase



Chase means to pursue a fleeing checker with the aim of hitting it. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Checker



Also called: Chequer, Counter, Man, Piece, Stone


Checker is one of the 15 playing pieces controlled by each player. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Chouette



Players use Chouette to describe a multiplayer format in which one player, the box, plays against a rotating team led by a captain. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Clean Play



Clean Play is a move that improves the position without leaving unnecessary blots or awkwardness. Knowing this term makes it easier to follow backgammon lessons and analysis.


Category: Checker Play and Tactics





Clear a Point



Clear a Point means to move every checker off a made point. The term gives players a shared way to talk about this part of the game.


Category: Board, Equipment, and Notation





Clear from the Rear



The action called Clear from the Rear is to move checkers first from the highest occupied points during bearoff or disengagement. It is useful vocabulary when describing a position, decision, rule, or result.


Category: Language, Rules, and Culture





Client Software



Client Software is the application a player uses to connect to an online backgammon service. Players may encounter the term when playing online or using a computer to study backgammon.


Category: Software and Online Play

Passing loses the current one-point stake.
Taking means continuing the game at a cube value of 2.
Under the simplified assumptions, taking and passing have equal value at the 25% boundary.
Taking is correct above the boundary and passing is correct below it.
Taking is not the same as predicting a win.
VERIFY: decide how the exact boundary should be described after notation is accepted.



Key idea

A take is not a prediction that you will win. It is a comparison between continuing at the doubled stake and surrendering the current stake.

title: Why Is 25% the Basic Take Point When a Double Is Offered?
text:
Why 25% appears

Passing

Passing ends the game immediately.
The player loses the current one-point stake.
This is the result that taking must be compared with.



Taking and winning

The game continues with the cube at 2.
A win gains two points in the simplified comparison.
The larger reward is why taking can be worthwhile even when winning is less likely.



Taking and losing

The game continues with the cube at 2.
A loss costs two points in the simplified comparison.
The player accepts this larger risk instead of surrendering one point immediately.



The decision boundary

At the boundary, taking and passing have the same value.
Above the boundary, continuing is worth more than passing.
Below the boundary, passing is worth more than continuing.

text: Sage and GNU played 20 seven-point matches using fixed ply depths and dice files prepared before play. Guess who won?

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
text:
At a glance

GNU 13 wins to Sage 7 wins. The binomial test says it is not statistically significant result.
4 ply review shows GNU with lower ER. Sage’s biggest differences were in Cube decisions.
4 ply review estimated that GNU was luckier, and received the more valuable rolls in every match

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
text:
Who won the matches?
GNU won 13 of the 20 matches. Sage won 7.

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
text:
Is GNU Better than Sage?
Unsure, the test was statisticaly insignificant. We need to run more matches.


What do you mean statistically insignificant? What test did you run?

If the engines were equal we would expect a 50% or 10 to 10 result. To judge the statistical significance, we asked a simple question:
If the engines had an equal chance of winning each match, given random chance, how often would we see a 13 to 7 result or better?
Using a two sided binomial test, the answer is about 26% of the time. Statisticians would say the study results show a p-value of 0.263. For the result to be significant, we would expect 5% or a p-value of 0.05. Therefore the 13-7 result is statistically insignificant. This does not mean there is a 26% chance that luck caused the result. It means the score, by itself, is not unusual enough to rule out an even matchup.
The TODO research page explains the test and shows the full distribution. You can also use this binomial-test calculator or watch this introduction to the binomial test if you are interested.


PENDING VALIDATED FIGURE :: MATCH SCORE AND 20-MATCH TILE STRIP
Show GNU with 13 wins and Sage with 7 wins. Add one chronological tile for each public match identifier. Do not use pair labels or A/B labels.

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
section: Did GNU have better rolls? How much did luck matter?
text:
Did GNU have better rolls? How much did luck matter?
Yes. GNU was luckier according to GNU’s 4-ply review. After adjusting for the rolls, 5 of GNU’s 13 wins no longer clearly showed GNU ahead. This makes the contest look closer than the official 13-7 score.


How was luck measured? And what would the result be after a luck adjustment?

The matches were reviewed at 4-ply, but GNU’s luck calculation uses a faster 0-ply evaluation. After each roll, it estimates how much better or worse the player’s position became, assuming the player then makes the best move according to that evaluation.
For a fuller explanation, read the classic article A Measure of Luck in Backgammon.
GNU’s review estimated that GNU received the more valuable rolls in all 20 matches. This does not mean the dice were biased or rigged. It means that, according to GNU’s calculation, the rolls improved GNU’s chances more than Sage’s.
The adjustment also estimates whether that roll advantage was large enough to affect which engine appeared ahead. All 7 of Sage’s wins still showed Sage ahead. Of GNU’s 13 wins, 8 still showed GNU ahead, 3 became nearly even, and 2 showed Sage ahead.
This adjustment is an estimate, not a replacement match score.


PENDING VALIDATED FIGURE :: WHAT CHANGED AFTER GNU’S ROLL ADJUSTMENT
Keep the two observed groups separate: the 7 Sage wins all still show Sage ahead; among the 13 GNU wins, 8 still show GNU ahead, 3 become nearly even, and 2 show Sage ahead. Do not combine them under a label such as winner remained ahead.



IMPORTANT LIMITATION
We used GNU 4 ply to review the matches and then a Sage rollout to resolve the arguments. GNU 4ply will of course favour GNU’s lower ply decisions.

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
section: How did the review rate the decisions?
text:
How did the review rate the decisions?
GNU had a lower ER. The difference in checker play was smaller, but Sage’s ER is much higher for Cube decisions.



Engine
Overall ER




Sage
1.416


GNU
0.154





How do you calculate ER?

After the matches, GNU compared each eligible checker and cube decision with the “best move”. It then estimated how much equity was lost by making the incorrect decision. Equity is the engine’s estimate of how valuable a position or decision is, based on the possible outcomes.
The way to calculate ER (Error Rate) is to take the sum of all equity loss (from the “mistakes”), divides it by the number of all non-forced decisions, and multiplies by 500. This produces the pooled error rate, or ER. Lower is better. We do not average the ER of the 20 matches. This is the same way BMAB calculates equity.
The Overall ER is calculated from the combined equity losses and all non-forced decisions. It is not the average of the 20 separate match ER values. A forced decision is for example when you roll while on the bar and not being able to come in, or when you are bearing in, there is only 1 available move. GNU review automatically calculates this, we do not.
In our case:
\[
\text{Sage ER}
=
500 \times \frac{4.735}{1{,}672}
=
1.416
\]
\[
\text{GNU ER}
=
500 \times \frac{0.523}{1{,}699}
=
0.154
\]

Show one directly labelled value for each engine, include a visible zero baseline, and state that lower is better. Equity loss and eligible-decision totals may appear as supporting text.

Where did the reviewed difference come from?
Most of the gap came from cube decisions.



Decision type
Sage ER
GNU ER

Cube decisions
9.652

GNU’s review found a relatively small difference in checker play and a much larger difference in cube decisions. Sage’s reviewed cube losses therefore account for most of its overall ER.
This does not prove that every disputed Sage cube decision was wrong. GNU made the judgment, and the separate Sage rollout study examines selected disagreements more deeply.

PENDING VALIDATED FIGURE :: CHECKER-PLAY AND CUBE-DECISION ER
Use separate panels and separate, clearly labelled scales. Show checker play as Sage 0.291 and GNU 0.177, and cube decisions as Sage 9.652 and GNU 0.021. State that lower is better.

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
section: How close were the checker plays?
text:
How close were the checker plays?
The ER values tell us the total reviewed loss. It also helps to ask how often each played move was very close to GNU’s preferred move.
GNU reports the gap on a normalized equity scale called EMG. EMG means equivilent money game, which is how we can compare the equity lost in different match formats. This is called “normalization”. To learn more, you can check out a class article on Normalizing Error.
Even 4 ply analysis doesn’t garuntee the correct move, so we considered if a checker decision was within 0.010 EMG equity of GNU’s preferred play, it to be the “correct” play.



Engine

Share




Sage

Both engines were close to 4 ply’s preferred move on the great majority of eligible checker decisions. This is not objective accuracy. It measures closeness to 4ply’s judgment.
A checker decision with zero reviewed loss stays in the total and counts as close. Zero-loss decisions may be left out of a separate plot of non-zero mistakes so the visible errors are easier to compare, but they are not removed from these percentages.

PENDING VALIDATED FIGURE :: CHECKER DECISIONS CLOSE TO GNU’S PREFERRED MOVE
Title the figure Checker decisions close to GNU’s preferred move. Show the percentages and raw counts, define the 0.010 EMG threshold, and avoid the words correct, incorrect, and accuracy.

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
text:
What about cube decisions?
Cube decisions need a separate calculation. There are far fewer eligible cube decisions, and routine no-double positions are not all included in the same way.
The final figure uses the same 0.010 equity EMG closeness threshold.

PENDING AUDITED FIGURE :: CUBE DECISIONS CLOSE TO GNU’S REVIEW
Show the share within 0.010 EMG and the share more than 0.010 EMG away, with percentages, raw counts, and the accepted eligible-decision total. State the zero rule in the subtitle or caption.

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
section: What happens when Sage and GNU disagree on the cube?
text:
What happens when Sage and GNU disagree on the cube?
GNU’s review found selected cube decisions where Sage’s original action differed from GNU’s recommendation.
Those positions are being examined with a deeper Sage rollout. In a rollout, Sage repeatedly plays forward from the same position to compare how the two actions perform over many continuations. Stage 1 compares only Sage’s original action with GNU’s recommendation. A rollout may support GNU, support Sage’s original action, or remain too close to call.

PENDING AUDITED SAGE ROLLOUT RESULTS
The public summary will be added after the audited rollout release is available. It will report completed and valid rollouts, results supporting each action, unresolved results, point-estimate-only results, and exclusions.


PENDING FIGURE :: SELECTED SAGE CUBE ROLLOUT RESULTS
Use only the audited two-action rollout release. Each published result must link to the position, match context, two actions, rollout settings, paired difference, valid uncertainty range when available, and any exclusion reason.

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
section: Why did the engines use different ply depths?
text:
Why did the engines use different ply depths?
A ply is one layer of lookahead. The engine examines a play, then a reply, then another reply as the ply depth increases.
GNU and Sage label those layers differently. GNU starts at 0-ply, while Sage starts at 1-ply. Giving both engines the same displayed number would therefore give them different amounts of lookahead.
Stage 1 used:
Checker play
GNU: 3-ply
Sage: 4-ply

Cube decisions
GNU: 2-ply
Sage: 3-ply
For checker play, these were the closest practical fixed-ply depths available in both engines.
For cube decisions, GNU 2-ply and Sage 3-ply both look ahead by both the player on roll and the reply by the opponent. If you use an odd number ply such as 3 ply for GNU, it only considers the player move and not the reply. To simplify, it makes a cube decisions where “riskier” moves are considered better because it isn’t looking for the reply of the opponent.
If that’s confusing, we explain it in detail in our research article
Matching the amount of lookahead makes the comparison fairer, but it does not make the engines identical. They still use different neural networks, cube models, move filters, and internal methods.

text: How long did it take to run?

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
section: How long did the matches and analysis take?
text:
How long did the matches and analysis take?
The live matches were fairly quick and consistent on our setup.
Figure 1
Figure 2
The match times were grouped fairly closely together. In technical terms, they had relatively low variance, meaning there was less difference between the shorter and longer matches.
The 4-ply review times were much more spread out. Although the average was just under 68 minutes, an individual review could take anywhere from just over 32 minutes to almost 2.5 hours. This made the analysis time much less predictable than the match time.
These results are specific our specific hardware and setup. For this pilot, we ran the live matches one at a time to reduce the risk of errors. We ran the 4-ply reviews in parallel, which allowed several completed matches to be analyzed at the same time.

title: Sage vs GNU: Stage 1
section: What does this study tell us?
text:
What does this study tell us?
In these 20 matches, GNU won more often and received the lower ER under GNU’s own post-match review. Most of the reviewed ER gap came from cube decisions. The checker plays of both engines were very often close to GNU’s preferred move.
GNU’s roll estimates suggest that the official 13-7 score may make the contest look more one-sided than it was. The adjusted result is still an estimate, not a corrected score. The cube-closeness percentage and Sage rollout conclusions also remain pending until their audited releases are ready.
This is evidence about these 20 matches, these engine versions, and these ply depths. It does not establish a permanent ranking between Sage and GNU.

title: About Backgammon Made Simple
text:
Backgammon Made Simple is an open-source project for understanding the game and making better decisions.
The idea is simple:

Come with a question. Leave with a clear mental model you can use at the board.

We try to make difficult ideas clearer, build useful tools, and help more people get excited about backgammon.


I started this project while trying to understand my own blunders. The engine gave me the best moves. A friend who is a great player said, “Eventually, you’ll start to see it.”
I wanted to know what I was supposed to see, as I asked questions like:

> Why is 25% often called the take point… and yet it rarely ever is?
> When should I run a lone back checker, move it up, or leave it where it is?
> Why is breaking an anchor brilliant one game and a blunder the next?
> What can one position teach me about the thousands I’ll see later?
// goal: clarity over perfection

Backgammon Made Simple is my attempt to answer questions with real positions, clear explanations, and evidence instead of folklore.

Hi, I’m Marty Gale, PhD.1
I research the intersection of dice rigging, probability, and questionable doubling decisions.
Behind the joke, Marty Gale is the public author identity for this project.
I am not presenting myself as one of the world’s great backgammon players. I am a curious player learning in public: asking questions, testing ideas, making mistakes, and trying to leave behind explanations that are more useful than a table of rollout results.

title: Backgammon Engine Benchmark
text:
The Backgammon Engine Benchmark lets engines play under controlled conditions, then publishes the results and the evidence behind them.
We ran a 20 match pilot with Sage vs GNU. After that pilot we wanted to release a robust way to fairly compare backgammon engines against each other. That’s why we built the Engine Benchmark tool.
Before you have backgammon engines fight each other, you must record the plan, settings, and how the dice were generated. You also want to record the match files, settings used for review and futher analysis . We do this for the comparison can be fair, inspected and reproduced by others.
The code and instructions to run your own tests is available in the public repository below, while the website has the stories of the battles we conducted and what it means for backgammon players like yourself.

title: Backgammon Engine Benchmark
text:
How the benchmark works


01 Choose the engines, rules, and settings


02 Publish the plan before play begins


04 Set Dice File then Play


05 Review the matches and find disagreements


06 Check and publish the evidence


You can configure the methods and settings as they can change from one study to another. Engines do not all offer the same tools, as some can review a complete match (GNU CLI), while others can only examine one position at a time (Sage’s current Python package).

title: Backgammon Engine Benchmark
section: Is the plan fixed before play?
text:
Is the plan fixed before play?
Yes.
Before the first match, we record the engine versions, match rules, ply depths, dice procedure, review method, and the questions the study will answer. This keeps the study from being changed after an early result.
A necessary change can still be made, but it is published as a change to the original plan, and the settings should be republished/comitted BEFORE the matches are run.

title: Backgammon Engine Benchmark
text:
Are the dice random?
No. The dice were deterministic.
The dice files were prepared before the matches using a pseudorandom number generator. Given the same generator, seeds, and preparation procedure, the same dice sequences can be recreated.
This is useful because a repeated study can use exactly the same dice rather than merely another random sample.

title: Backgammon Engine Benchmark
text:
How are engine settings matched?
Engine settings cannot always be matched by using the same ply number.
Ply depth tells us how many decision layers an engine looks ahead. Different engines start count plying depth differently, use different types of search, or expose different analysis tools. Before a study begins, you want to documents what each setting does understand why the selected pair is the closest practical comparison.
The goal is not to make the engines internally identical. That is impossible. The goal is to avoid an obvious mismatch in ply depth while keeping the live matches practical to run.
Read the more details of ply settings for the Pilot

title: Backgammon Engine Benchmark
text:
How are the results judged?

Match wins and decision quality are different
The score tells us who won, and a binomial test can see if it’s statistically significant.
A review from a stronger engine (or engine setting) looks at the choices made during the match.
This distinction matters because an engine can make stronger decisions and still lose after receiving worse rolls. The benchmark therefore presents the score, decision review, and estimated “luck” /roll advantage as separate evidence.


The reviewer is named
We use GNU 4ply to review the decisions made by both engines. The same review method was used for both sides, which keeps the scoring consistent.
Sage doesn’t offer a match review function in it’s current Python package. We decided not to implement one as it could be error prone. Instead we just use the GNU 4 ply to evaluate matches, and compore the differences using a Sage rollout (explained in the next section)
Using GNU 4ply as a review means that it can not be considered a neutral source of perfect answers. It’s lower ply cousin also competed in the matches, and it’s likely to favour those moves at higher ply as well. The results are therefore described as GNU’s estimates, not as proof of the objectively correct decision.
We ideally would be able to BGBlitz or XG, and will be future work if we can get permission from the developers. This is always a challenge with open-source projects unfortunately. This doesn’t stop you from reviewing the match files we publish in bulk and letting us know what you find! We can publish your results too!


Some disagreements receive a deeper look
A normal match review can find positions where Sage and GNU preferred different actions. These positions can then be examined more deeply by playing out many possible continuations from the same position. This is called a rollout.
Best practice (since GNU is reviewing) is for Sage to do a rollout for the positions which GNU 4 ply said was “wrong”. We can then look at the positions and consider outselves what is the best move. Or ask another engine.

title: Backgammon Engine Benchmark
text:
What is checked and published?
The project keeps the evidence needed to follow the comparison from the original plan to the public result. This includes the engine versions and settings, prepared dice, completed match files, review files, selected positions, deeper analysis, and validation reports.
The important checks are also recorded. We confirm that the intended engines and rules were used, the matches completed, the published totals match the source files, and the deeper analysis used the stated positions and settings. Failed checks, retries, and exclusions are not silently removed.
The public website explains the findings. The repository keeps the more detailed record for readers who want to inspect or repeat the work.

title: Backgammon Engine Benchmark
section: What can the benchmark tell us?
text:
What can the benchmark tell us?
A study can show what happened between specific engine versions under specific rules and settings. It can also show how a named reviewer judged their decisions and what deeper analysis found in selected disagreements.
It cannot prove that one engine is always stronger. Backgammon results are affected by the rolls, reviewers can disagree, and different settings can produce different behaviour. Larger studies can provide stronger evidence, but every conclusion still belongs to the conditions that were tested.

title: Backgammon Engine Benchmark
text:
What comes next?
We are going onto Stage 1 where we will test the full process with a small set of matches. The same approach can later be used for larger studies, different settings, and other engines.
Each new study will publish its plan before play and keep its results separate, so readers can see exactly which evidence supports each conclusion.

title: What the Cube Is Really Asking
text:
The Simple Answer
The cube turns a position into a decision about risk, reward, and timing.

section: How the study was set up
text:
How the study was set up

Four questions, four kinds of evidence
The final score, the decision review, the roll estimate, and the deeper Sage rollouts answer different questions.







Question
Evidence used




Who won the matches?
The completed match results


How did GNU rate the decisions?
GNU’s post-match review of checker and cube decisions


How much did the rolls appear to matter?
GNU’s estimate of the value added by the rolls


What happens when selected cube disagreements are examined more deeply?
Sage rollouts comparing two specified actions



These results are shown separately. They are not combined into one final engine-strength score.


Match structure
The pilot ran 20 individual seven-point matches. We generated the dice files before the matches were run.
We did not take note of the exact model versions, and all of the settings in a reliable way. That’s why we built engine benchmark so for future runs anyone can rerun the analysis.


Study identifiers and analysis unit

Study ID: sage-gnu-stage1-public-analysis-v1
Matches: 20
Match length: 7 points
Public identifiers: match_001 through match_020
Primary match-result unit: one completed match



Were the dice random?
No. The dice were deterministic.
The dice files were prepared before the matches using a pseudorandom number generator. Given the same generator, seeds, and preparation procedure, the same dice sequences can be recreated.
This is useful because a repeated study can use exactly the same dice rather than merely another random sample.


Were the dice rigged?
No.
The dice files were fixed before play. They were not changed after seeing the engines’ decisions or results, and they were not selected to help either engine.
The generator details, seeds, dice files, checksums, settings, and match files are retained so the setup can be inspected or repeated. The historical seat swaps did not create common-dice pairs, so this analysis does not assume that luck cancels between two matches.

title: Sage vs GNU: Additional Details
text:
Ply Settings
We used the default ply settings and did not used any custom configs such as move filter settings.

Checker-play ply depths
The live checker-play depths were:
GNU checker play: 3-ply
Sage checker play: 4-ply
These were the closest practical regular fixed-ply depths available through the two engine interfaces. Sage 4-ply was its strongest regular fixed-ply checker option in the interface used for this study.
GNU 4-ply was kept for the post-match review rather than live play because it took substantially longer on this setup.


Cube-decision ply depths
The live cube depths were:
GNU cube decisions: 2-ply
Sage cube decisions: 3-ply

title: Sage vs GNU: Additional Details
section: Why these ply depths were chosen?
text:
Why these ply depths were chosen?
A ply is one layer of lookahead. As the ply depth increases, an engine examines a play, the reply, and further replies before rating the resulting position.
GNU and Sage label those layers differently. GNU starts at 0-ply, while Sage starts at 1-ply. Giving both engines the same displayed number would therefore give them different amounts of lookahead.
GNU 0-ply ~= Sage 1-ply
GNU 1-ply ~= Sage 2-ply
GNU 2-ply ~= Sage 3-ply
GNU 3-ply ~= Sage 4-ply
The goal was not to make the engines internally identical. They use different neural networks, cube models, move filters, bearoff methods, and internal procedures. The narrower goal was to avoid an obvious mismatch in ply depth while keeping the live matches practical to run and possible to repeat.

What are move filters?
Looking several plies ahead takes a great deal of time. To make deeper analysis fast enough for live play, an engine does not always carry every legal checker move through the full search.
Instead, it gives all the moves a quicker first evaluation. The moves that look most promising continue to the deeper search, while moves that appear clearly worse are removed. This shortcut is called a move filter.
GNU and Sage both use move filters, but they do not use exactly the same system. GNU’s filters control how many moves continue at each stage and how close an additional move must be to the current leader. Sage also ranks the moves at a lower ply depth, keeps a limited group near the best preliminary result, and then analyzes those moves more deeply.
A wider filter examines more moves and usually takes longer. A tighter filter is faster, but there is a greater chance that a move removed during the quick evaluation would have looked better after the full search.
For Stage 1, we matched the main ply depths, but we did not separately configure or match the move filters. The run relied on the filtering supplied by each engine’s tested version and run configuration. This helped keep the live matches practical, but it also means that matching ply depth did not make the two searches identical.
The study therefore compares the complete engine configurations that were actually used. It cannot tell us whether a difference came from the neural network, the move filter, the deeper search, or another part of the engine. A future study should record the active move-filter settings and could test wider filters to see whether the results change.
This pairing lets the player on roll have one examined turn and then lets the opponent have one examined reply before the position is evaluated.

Why not use a shallower or deeper cube pairing?

The shallower pairing, GNU 1-ply and Sage 2-ply, stops after the player on roll has moved. It does not examine the opponent’s reply. An immediate hit, escape, attack, or point may therefore look better before the engine checks whether the opponent can answer it.
The next deeper pairing, GNU 3-ply and Sage 4-ply, gives the original player two examined turns but gives the opponent only one. GNU 4-ply would give both players two turns, but Sage did not offer a matching regular 5-ply live option.
GNU 2-ply and Sage 3-ply were therefore the least uneven practical pairing for live cube decisions.

title: Sage vs GNU: Additional Details
text:
Match results

Who won?
GNU won 13 of the 20 matches. Sage won 7.

PENDING FIGURE :: MATCH SCORE AND 20-MATCH TILE STRIP
Show GNU with 13 wins and Sage with 7 wins. Add one chronological tile for each public match identifier, with no A/B or pair labels.




How strong was the 13-7 result?
If the engines were equally likely to win each match, a 13-7 split in either direction, or a wider gap, would occur about 26% of the time.
The formal result is a two-sided binomial p-value of 0.263. Because this is above the study’s 0.05 threshold, the score alone was not strong enough evidence to rule out an even matchup.
This does not mean there is a 26% chance that luck caused the result. It also does not mean there is a 74% chance that GNU is stronger.


See the test inputs and threshold

Number of matches: 20
GNU wins: 13
Sage wins: 7
Null GNU win probability: 0.5
Test: two-sided binomial
p-value: 0.26317596435546875
Study threshold: 0.05
Fifteen GNU wins is the first result on that side to fall below the 0.05 threshold. Its two-sided p-value is about 0.041. The threshold is a research convention, not a point at which a result becomes certain.


PENDING FIGURE :: TWO-SIDED BINOMIAL DISTRIBUTION
Show GNU win totals from 0 through 20 under a 50% win probability. Mark the observed 13 wins and both tails used for the p-value. Also mark 15 wins as the first GNU total below the 0.05 threshold.




Did GNU have better rolls? How much did luck matter?
Yes. GNU was luckier according to GNU’s review. That makes the official 13-7 score look more one-sided than the underlying contest may have been.
After GNU’s estimated roll advantage was removed, all 7 Sage wins still showed Sage ahead. Of GNU’s 13 wins, 8 still showed GNU ahead, 3 became nearly even, and 2 showed Sage ahead.
Twenty matches are not enough to settle the comparison, so a longer test is needed.
Open the explanation below to see how luck was estimated, or keep scrolling for the graphs.


How was luck measured, and what changed after the adjustment?

The completed matches were reviewed at 4-ply. GNU’s luck calculation itself uses a faster 0-ply evaluation after each roll. It estimates how much better or worse the player’s position became, assuming the player then makes the move preferred by that evaluation.
For more background, read the classic article A Measure of Luck in Backgammon.
GNU estimated that it received the more valuable rolls in all 20 matches. This does not mean the dice were biased or rigged. It means that, according to GNU’s calculation, the rolls improved GNU’s chances more than Sage’s in the positions that occurred.
The adjustment also estimates whether the roll advantage was large enough to change which engine appeared ahead. All 7 Sage wins still showed Sage ahead. Among GNU’s 13 wins, 8 still showed GNU ahead, 3 became nearly even, and 2 showed Sage ahead.
This is a model-based estimate. It does not replay the matches, decide who deserved to win, or create a replacement match score.



How is the adjusted result centered?

GNU starts with a centered result and subtracts its estimate of the net dice advantage:
Observed win:  +50
Observed loss: -50
Zero:          neutral adjusted result
These are analytical values centered on zero. They are not literal final match-winning chances of 100% and 0%.
The report labels an adjusted result within plus or minus 1 match-winning-chance percentage point as nearly even. This is an editorial band, not a confidence interval or a statistical test.

Show all 20 matches: 7 Sage wins that still show Sage ahead, 8 GNU wins that still show GNU ahead, 3 GNU wins that become nearly even, and 2 GNU wins that show Sage ahead after adjustment. Use only the direct GNU centered adjusted result.

Equity is the value of a position or decision after accounting for the possible match outcomes. An error rate, or ER, summarizes the estimated equity lost per eligible decision. Lower is better.
The same reviewer and review configuration were used for both engines, which keeps the calculation consistent. GNU still remains both competitor and reviewer.

section: How selected cube disagreements are being checked
text:
How selected cube disagreements are being checked
GNU’s review identified selected cube positions where Sage’s original action differed from GNU’s recommendation.
Those positions are examined with a deeper Sage rollout. A rollout repeatedly plays forward from the same position to compare how two actions perform across many possible continuations.
Stage 1 compares exactly two actions: Sage’s original cube action and GNU’s recommendation. A valid uncertainty range entirely on GNU’s side supports GNU. A range entirely on Sage’s side supports Sage’s original action. A range that includes zero is unresolved. A point estimate without a valid paired uncertainty range is reported separately and is not called resolved.
No conclusion is made about a third action.

PENDING AUDITED SAGE ROLLOUT RELEASE
Do not publish rollout verdicts, counts, or representative positions until the audited rollout release is available. Pending does not mean zero.



What must the audited rollout section include?

The final section must show how many positions were selected, attempted, completed, valid, resolved, unresolved, point-estimate-only, and excluded. It must report how many valid results support GNU and how many support Sage’s original action.
Each published position must include the exact match context, the two actions, the paired Sage difference in EMG, its valid uncertainty range when available, the classification, the rollout settings and trial count, and a link to the retained evidence.
The interpretation must stay within the selected positions. It must not claim that Sage’s neural evaluator is generally weaker unless a separate experiment isolates that cause.

Independent validation
The study checks that the intended engines, models, rules, cube settings, ply depths, and dice evidence were used. It also checks that the matches completed, the review settings are supported, the denominators and totals are correct, the roll orientation is consistent, and the rollout positions and actions are aligned correctly.
Figures are checked against the accepted tables, including their values, labels, units, captions, and alternative text. When practical, the person validating the release is separate from the person who produced it.


What is kept so the study can be repeated?

The public record should include the source-code commits, engine versions and models, ply depths, match rules, cube settings, dice-generation inputs, retained stream evidence, run commands, environment details, original match and review files, the audited analytical release, Sage rollout evidence, figure-to-table mappings, validation reports, retries, exclusions, manifests, and checksums.

Limitations







Limitation
Why it matters




Small sample
Twenty matches are not enough to establish a stable ranking. The 13-7 score did not meet the study’s 0.05 threshold.


One tested setup
The findings apply to these engine versions, models, ply depths, match rules, and hardware. Other setups may give different results.


Independent dice streams
The historical seat swaps were not common-dice pairs, so the analysis does not assume paired luck cancellation.


GNU was competitor and reviewer
Using one reviewer keeps the arithmetic consistent, but GNU may favour decisions that resemble its own methods.


Match ER is descriptive
Match-level ER helps show variation but is not the official pooled estimate or an independent sample for inference.


Roll adjustments are model-based
The adjusted result depends on GNU’s evaluation. It is not a replay, corrected score, or proof of who should have won.


Presentation bands are not statistical tests
The 0.010 EMG closeness threshold and the plus or minus 1 MWC nearly-even band are reporting rules, not confidence intervals.


Rollouts cover selected positions
The Sage rollout results apply to the chosen cube disagreements and should not be generalized to every Sage decision.


The evaluator was not isolated
This study cannot separate the neural evaluator from ply depth, move filters, cube modelling, and other engine components.

title: Sage vs GNU: Additional Details
text:
What the evidence supports
GNU won more of these 20 matches, but the 13-7 score was not strong enough to cross the study’s statistical threshold.
GNU’s own review gave GNU the lower pooled ER, with most of the reviewed difference coming from cube decisions. Both engines were very often within 0.010 EMG of GNU’s preferred checker move.
GNU estimated that it received the more valuable rolls in all 20 matches. The adjusted categories suggest that the official score may have made the contest look more one-sided than it was, but they do not create a corrected score.
The cube-closeness percentage and Sage rollout conclusions remain pending until their audited releases are available.
This is a reproducible descriptive pilot about these matches and this tested setup. It does not establish a universal or permanent ranking of Sage and GNU.
